items.prompt: A login page correctly rejects wrong passwords, but the /admin endpoint accepts any request from anyone who is logged in, admin or not. What's missing?
choices: Nothing — accepting any logged-in user is correct behavior
The endpoint checked authentication but never checked authorization — being logged in as *someone* isn't the same as being allowed to reach /admin
The login page itself is broken
This is only a bug if the password is stored in plain text
items.explanation: This is exactly the bug class the unit warns about: authentication (who are you) and authorization (what are you allowed to do) are separate checks, and an endpoint that only performs the first one is vulnerable regardless of how well login itself is implemented.
items.reference:
🪪 Authentication

who are you

🚪 Authorization

what can you do

Why: a system can correctly verify identity and still have a bug that grants access it shouldn't.
items.learnMore:
Authentication vs. authorization

Two questions a request has to answer, checked independently.

AuthenticationAuthorization

Common mistake

Assuming a logged-in session implies permission for every action it can reach. Each endpoint needs its own authorization check, not a blanket "they're logged in, so it's fine."

items.prompt: What's the distinction between authentication and authorization?
choices: They're two names for the same thing
Authentication answers "who are you"; authorization answers "what are you allowed to do" — a system can correctly verify identity and still have a bug that grants access it shouldn't
Authentication is for web apps, authorization is for mobile apps
Authorization always happens before authentication in a correct system
items.explanation: These are explicitly separate questions. A real, common bug class is an endpoint that checks whether a request is authenticated (logged in as someone) but never separately checks whether that specific someone is authorized for the specific action being requested.

Logging in proves identity, not permission — a logged-in user might still be the wrong user for a specific action, which authentication alone can't catch

items.prompt: Why should a password be hashed rather than encrypted for storage?
choices: Encryption is always slower than hashing, so hashing is preferred purely for performance

A password only ever needs to be verified, never retrieved — encryption is deliberately reversible (right for data you need back), while hashing is deliberately one-way, which matches what a password actually needs
Hashing and encryption are the same operation with different names
Encrypted passwords can't be checked against a login attempt at all, so encryption is technically impossible to use
items.explanation: The reversibility of encryption is exactly the wrong property for a password: the system never needs the original value back, only needs to confirm a login attempt matches it — a one-way hash provides that without ever storing anything that could be reversed into the real password.
items.reference:
EncryptionHashing
Reversible?Yes, with a keyNo, by design
Right forData you need backData you only verify

Why: a password only ever needs to be checked, never retrieved.
items.learnMore:
Hashing vs. encryption

Both transform data, but for opposite purposes.

HashingEncryption
Reversible?NoYes, with the key
Right forData only ever verifiedData you need back
Password use caseCorrect primitiveWrong primitive

Common mistake

Choosing encryption because it "feels" more secure-sounding, or because support wants to look passwords up. Needing to look up the real value is itself the sign the wrong primitive was chosen.

items.prompt: Company C stores passwords "encrypted" so support staff can look them up when a user forgets. What does this reveal about their design?
choices: Nothing wrong — encryption is the correct choice for passwords

They chose a reversible primitive for data that should never need to be reversed — the ability to "look up" a password is itself the vulnerability, since anyone with the key (an attacker included, if it's ever compromised) can do the same
This is fine as long as the encryption key is long enough
Hashing would make lookup impossible, so encryption is required here
items.explanation: The need to "look up" a real password is a symptom that the wrong primitive was chosen. A system should only ever need to verify a password, never retrieve it — a hashed password can't be looked up by anyone, including support staff or an attacker.

items.prompt: If a password's stored form can be turned back into the real password by someone holding the right key, what primitive was used?
choices: Hashing
Encryption — reversibility by design is exactly what a key enables, and exactly what a password's storage should never allow
Salting
Constant-time comparison
items.explanation: Reversibility is the defining property of encryption, not hashing. A password's stored form should never be reversible by anyone, key or no key — that's the entire reason hashing, not encryption, is the right primitive.

items.prompt: Which of these is NOT one of the three traditional authentication factor categories?
choices: Something you know
Something you have
Something you are
Something you did yesterday
items.explanation: The three traditional categories are something you know (a password), something you have (a phone or key), and something you are (a fingerprint or face). "Something you did" isn't one of them.
items.reference:
🧠 Something you know — a password
📱 Something you have — a phone, a key
👆 Something you are — a fingerprint, a face

Why: real MFA combines categories, not duplicates within one.
items.learnMore:
The three authentication factor categories

Every credential fits into exactly one of these, and MFA means spanning more than one.

CategoryExample
KnowPassword, PIN, security questionMemorized secret
HavePhone, hardware key, ID cardPhysical possession
AreFingerprint, face, voiceBiological trait

Common mistake

Treating "two credentials" as automatically MFA without checking whether they're actually from different categories — two memorized secrets is still one factor.

items.prompt: A fingerprint scan falls into which authentication factor category?
choices: Something you know
Something you have
Something you are — a biological trait, not a memorized secret or a possessed object
Something you did
items.explanation: A fingerprint is a biological trait the person inherently has, distinct from a memorized secret (something you know) or a physical object (something you have) — it's the "something you are" category.

items.prompt: A system requires both a password AND a security question (another memorized secret) before login. Is this multi-factor authentication?
choices: Yes — two credentials means two factors
No — both are "something you know," so this is still single-factor with an extra step, not true MFA, which requires combining different categories
Yes, as long as the security question is hard to guess
No, because security questions are never secure regardless of category
items.explanation: MFA specifically means combining different categories, not requiring multiple things from the same one. Two memorized secrets are both "something you know" — still one factor, just checked twice.
items.reference:
🧠 Something you know — a password
📱 Something you have — a phone, a key
👆 Something you are — a fingerprint, a face

Why: real MFA combines categories, not duplicates within one.

Trap: two passwords is still just one factor — "know" twice.
items.learnMore:
Why category matters for MFA

MFA's security value comes from an attacker needing to defeat fundamentally different kinds of defenses, not just more of the same kind.

AttackReal MFA resistance
Stolen password + guessed security questionBoth defeated by the same skill: social engineering / guessingWeak
Stolen password + stolen phoneRequires two separate compromises of different kindsStrong

Common mistake

Believing any second step automatically strengthens security. A second memorized secret is defeated by the same class of attack (phishing, guessing) as the first.

PIN + a memorized security question
Two different memorized passphrases
items.explanation: A password (something you know) combined with a phone-delivered code (something you have) crosses categories — that's what makes it genuine MFA, unlike stacking two memorized secrets.

items.prompt: Per this unit's opening scenario, why did Company A have to force a password reset for all 2 million users while Company B didn't?
choices: Company B had fewer users
Company A stored plain text passwords — the attacker read every real password directly; Company B's salted hashes gave the attacker nothing directly usable
Company A used a weaker firewall
Both companies had to reset passwords equally
items.explanation: The gap traces entirely to the storage decision made before the breach: plain text is never transformed, so a stolen copy is every real password; a salted hash is not directly usable by an attacker, so nothing needs to change for Company B's users.
items.reference:
🔓 Company A — plain text

all 2M passwords readable instantly

🔒 Company B — salted hash

0 passwords directly recovered
items.learnMore:
What a breach actually exposes, by storage method

The storage decision made long before a breach determines what a stolen database is worth to an attacker.

Protection at restAttacker's immediate gain
Plain textNone — never transformedEvery password, instantly
Salted hashOne-way, unique per userNothing directly usable

Common mistake

Judging password security only by login-time behavior (rate limiting, lockouts) while ignoring how the password is stored — storage is what determines the blast radius of a breach.

items.prompt: If a database storing passwords in plain text is stolen, how many of those passwords does the attacker recover?
choices: None — plain text still requires cracking
Roughly half, on average
All of them, immediately, with no cracking required — plain text was never transformed in the first place
Only the passwords shorter than 8 characters
items.explanation: Plain text means exactly what it says: nothing was hashed, encrypted, or otherwise transformed, so a stolen copy of the database is a stolen copy of every real password, instantly and completely.

items.prompt: Two users both choose the password "password123", and the system uses per-user random salts. Will their stored hashes be identical?
choices: Yes — identical passwords always produce identical hashes

No — because each user's salt is different, hash(password + salt) produces a different result even for the identical password, which is exactly what defeats a precomputed rainbow table from cracking both users via one lookup
Yes, but only if they registered on the same day
No, but only because scrypt is inherently randomized regardless of salting
items.explanation: Salting's entire purpose is breaking the identical-input-identical-output property for password hashing specifically — with unique per-user salts, a precomputed table would have to be redone per salt, eliminating the economic advantage of precomputing at all.
items.reference:
Unsalted: same password → same hash → 1 lookup cracks every matching user
Salted: same password → different hash per user → precompute defeated
items.learnMore:
What salting actually breaks

Salting exists to remove one specific property: identical input producing identical output.

Salted?Formula
Nohash(password)Same for every user with that password
Yeshash(password + per-user salt)Unique per user, even for shared passwords

Common mistake

Thinking salting makes the hash function itself stronger or slower. It doesn't — it changes the input, not the algorithm's speed or one-way-ness.

items.prompt: An attacker builds a rainbow table mapping common passwords to their SHA-256 hashes, with no salting anywhere in the target system. How many users sharing a common password does one table lookup crack?
choices: Just one, the specific target
All of them at once — an unsalted hash is identical for identical passwords, so one precomputed lookup cracks every user who happens to share that password
None, because rainbow tables only work on encrypted data
It depends on how long ago the table was built
items.explanation: Without salting, the hash function's output depends only on the password — so every user sharing a password shares a hash, and one precomputed lookup cracks all of them simultaneously.
items.reference:
Unsalted: same password → same hash → 1 lookup cracks every matching user
Salted: same password → different hash per user → precompute defeated

It makes the output shorter
It makes the output depend on more than just the password, so identical passwords across users no longer produce identical hashes
It removes the need to store anything alongside the hash
items.explanation: Salting doesn't change the hash function's speed or output length — it changes the *input*, tying the output to a per-user random value in addition to the password, which is what breaks the identical-password-identical-hash relationship.

items.prompt: A team salts every password with the same hardcoded string `'s4lt!'` before hashing. Does this stop a rainbow-table attack?
choices: Completely — any salt at all is sufficient

Only against a *generic* precomputed table — an attacker who knows (or guesses) that fixed salt can precompute one table targeting it, cracking every user at once, which defeats the actual purpose of salting
No, hardcoded salts have zero effect on anything
Yes, but only for passwords shorter than the salt itself
items.explanation: A shared, hardcoded salt still blocks a generic table built with no salt assumption — but it's a single fixed value an attacker can target directly, at which point one precomputation effort cracks every user, exactly like having no salt at all.
items.reference:
A single shared/hardcoded salt still blocks a *generic* rainbow table—

—but a table built to target that one known salt cracks every user at once. Protection requires a salt unique per user, generated randomly.
items.learnMore:
A salt is only as good as its uniqueness

"Using a salt" and "using a salt correctly" are different claims.

Blocks generic tables?Blocks targeted attack?
Yes, if attacker doesn't know itNo — one target cracks everyoneShared/hardcoded salt
YesYesPer-user random salt

Common mistake

Treating "we use a salt" as a finished security claim without checking whether it's random and unique per user — a fixed salt is a known quantity an attacker can target directly.

items.prompt: What's the difference between a properly implemented per-user salt and a single shared "pepper" baked into the code?
choices: There is no difference — both are called salting

A per-user salt means cracking one user's hash tells an attacker nothing about any other user's; a single shared value means one successful precomputation effort (targeting that value) cracks every user at once
A pepper is always longer than a salt
Peppers are only used for encryption, not hashing
items.explanation: The protection salting provides is per-user isolation: breaking one hash shouldn't help crack any other. A single shared value collapses that isolation back down to "one attack cracks everyone," the exact failure mode salting exists to prevent.

items.prompt: After a user logs in successfully, why does the server stop checking their password on every subsequent request?
choices: It doesn't — the password is re-hashed and compared on every request
A session/token issued at login stands in for "this request already proved identity" — the password is only ever involved at the initial login, not on every request after
Passwords are only checked once per day regardless of how many requests are made
This is a security flaw that most systems accidentally have
items.explanation: The whole point of a session/token is to avoid re-proving identity on every request — the password is checked exactly once, at login, and the token stands in for that proof afterward.
items.reference:
1. Password checked — once, at login
2. Hash compared to stored hash
3. Token issued
4. Token presented on every later request

Why: protecting the token is a separate problem from protecting the password.
items.learnMore:
The authentication chain has more than one link

A vulnerability doesn't have to live in the password-hashing step at all.

Chain linkTypical failure
Login (once)Weak hashing, no saltPassword compromise
Every request afterInsecure storage, no expiry, no revocationToken compromise

Common mistake

Auditing only the password-hashing code and assuming the system is secure, while the token that actually authorizes every later request is stored in an insecure place or never expires.

items.prompt: Why is "protecting the session token" considered a genuinely separate security problem from "protecting the password"?
choices: It isn't — they're the same problem with different names

Because the token has its own distinct failure modes (how it's stored client-side, whether it's sent over plain HTTP, how long it stays valid, whether it can be revoked) that have nothing to do with how the password itself was hashed or salted
Because tokens are never sent over the network
Because passwords expire but tokens never do
items.explanation: Hashing and salting only protect the password at the moment it's stored and checked. Once a token exists, an entirely different set of concerns takes over — transport security, storage, expiry, revocation — independent of how well the original password was protected.

items.prompt: A stolen session token, without the corresponding password, is enough for an attacker to do what?

Impersonate that user for as long as the token remains valid — the whole point of a token is to stand in for proof of identity on every request after login
Only read that user's public profile, never act as them
Reset that user's password automatically

items.prompt: Login verification re-hashes the entered password with the stored salt and compares it to the stored hash. For this to ever succeed, what property must the hash function have?
choices: It must be reversible
It must be deterministic — the exact same input (password + salt) must always produce the exact same output, or a correct password could fail to match its own stored hash
It must run in constant time
It must produce a different output every time, even for the same input
items.explanation: Verification only works because hashing is deterministic: hashing the same password with the same salt always reproduces the exact same value that was stored at registration. Without that, even the correct password would sometimes fail to match.
items.reference:
StepNeeds to be
Salt generation (once, at registration)Random
Hashing (every login)Deterministic
items.learnMore:
Randomness once, determinism forever after

These aren't in tension — they apply to different moments in the same flow.

StepRequirement
Once, at registrationMust be randomUnpredictability, ties hash to this user
Every loginMust be deterministicSame input always reproduces the same stored hash

Common mistake

Assuming "secure" always means "random" — a hash function that produced a different output for the same password+salt every time would make login verification impossible, not more secure.

items.prompt: Salt generation is supposed to be random and unpredictable at registration time — but the hash function applied afterward must be the opposite: deterministic. Why isn't this a contradiction?
choices: It is a contradiction — one of the two claims is wrong

They apply to two different steps: the salt only needs to be random *once*, at generation; after that, hashing the same password+salt combination must reliably reproduce the same result every login, or verification would never work
Randomness and determinism are the same property described differently
The hash function is only deterministic the first time it's used
items.explanation: Randomness and determinism apply at different moments: the salt is generated randomly once, then treated as a fixed input from then on — the hash function itself must always behave deterministically given that (now-fixed) salt and a password.

Hashing (every login)Deterministic

items.prompt: Why is being "cryptographically one-way" not sufficient on its own for a password hash?
choices: One-way-ness is actually irrelevant to password security
Speed matters independently of one-way-ness — a fast one-way hash still lets an attacker try billions of guesses per second against a stolen hash, which a deliberately slow function prevents
One-way functions are always slow by definition
This only matters for passwords shorter than 12 characters
items.explanation: One-way-ness only means the hash can't be reversed directly — it says nothing about how cheap it is to test guesses. A fast one-way hash is still weak against brute force; a deliberately slow one raises the cost of every single guess.
items.reference:
Fast (SHA-256)

billions of guesses/sec

Slow (scrypt/bcrypt/Argon2)

tens of guesses/sec, tunable lower
items.learnMore:
Speed is a defense, not just a performance number

One-way-ness and speed are independent properties — a hash function needs the right combination of both for passwords specifically.

Guesses per second (approx.)Example
Billions/secSHA-256, MD5Fast hash
Tens/sec, tunable lowerscrypt, bcrypt, Argon2Slow KDF

Common mistake

Choosing a hash function based only on "is it one-way" and ignoring speed — a fast one-way hash is still a poor password hash, because speed is what makes brute-forcing cheap.

items.prompt: What's the actual trade-off a slow key-derivation function (scrypt/bcrypt/Argon2) makes, compared to a fast general-purpose hash?
choices: It trades security for speed

It trades a small, imperceptible cost at real login time for a much larger cost per guess for an attacker brute-forcing a stolen hash — the same slowness that costs the real user milliseconds costs the attacker the same milliseconds per guess, at scale
It trades hash length for security
There is no trade-off — slow functions are strictly worse
items.explanation: The trade-off runs in the defender's favor: a real user pays the slow-hash cost once, imperceptibly, per login; an attacker pays that same cost per guess, and guesses number in the billions — which is where the real protection comes from.

items.prompt: Per L3, why does comparing two hashes with a normal `===`/byte-by-byte comparison (instead of a constant-time comparison) create a real vulnerability?

=== is simply slower than timingSafeEqual, with no security implication
This only matters for hashes longer than 256 bits
items.explanation: This is a timing side-channel: early-exit comparison leaks partial-match information through response time. timingSafeEqual always takes the same time regardless of where (or whether) a mismatch occurs, closing that channel — a subtle but real vulnerability class distinct from the hashing algorithm itself.

items.prompt: In L3's rainbow-table demo, `user1Hash === user2Hash` evaluates to `true` for two different users. What made that possible?
choices: A bug in the demo code
Both users chose the identical password and the hash was unsalted — identical input to an unsalted hash function always produces identical output
SHA-256 has hash collisions between different passwords
The demo used encryption instead of hashing
items.explanation: Unsalted hashing means the output depends only on the password. Two identical passwords, hashed the same unsalted way, produce byte-identical hashes — exactly what the demo shows.
items.reference:
Unsalted: user1Hash === user2Hash → true
One rainbowTable.get() lookup cracks both
Salted: salted1 === salted2 → false
items.learnMore:
The rainbow table attack, mechanically

The attack is entirely offline and precomputed — the target system is never touched until the final lookup.

StepWhat happens
1Precompute hash for every common password (once, offline)No target needed yet
2Compare precomputed table against stolen hash(es)Instant crack for any match

Common mistake

Thinking the attack requires guessing against the live system (which rate-limiting would slow down). The expensive work happens entirely offline, before the breach — rate limiting doesn't touch it.

items.prompt: In the same demo, one `rainbowTable.get()` lookup successfully returns the password for both `user1Hash` and `user2Hash`. What does this prove about the economics of the attack?
choices: That the attacker had to do twice the work for two users
That a single precomputed table cracks every user sharing that password at once — the attacker's cost doesn't scale with the number of victims, only with the number of distinct passwords in the table
That SHA-256 is fundamentally broken as a hash function
That the demo requires access to the real database to work
items.explanation: The precomputation is done once, offline, with no target needed — after that, cracking any user who shares a password with the table is a free lookup, which is exactly why the attack scales so cheaply against unsalted hashes.

items.prompt: Why does the unit warn against hand-rolling a custom authentication scheme, given that salting, slow hashing, and constant-time comparison are each individually simple?
choices: It doesn't — hand-rolling is encouraged once you understand the pieces

Simplicity of each individual piece is exactly what makes the whole system tempting to hand-roll — but a single subtle mistake in any one piece (a salt that isn't truly random, a comparison that isn't truly constant-time) silently reintroduces the vulnerability, often undiscovered until exploited
Custom schemes are always slower than library implementations
Audited libraries are only necessary for encryption, not hashing
items.explanation: Each mechanism being conceptually simple doesn't mean it's simple to implement correctly under every condition — a subtle flaw in any single piece can quietly undo the whole system's protection, which is why audited, widely-scrutinized libraries are preferred over from-scratch implementations.
items.reference:
✅ Salting — easy to get subtly wrong (non-random salt)
✅ Slow hashing — easy to under-tune
✅ Constant-time compare — easy to accidentally short-circuit
✅ Audited library — many eyes already found these mistakes
items.learnMore:

Common mistake

Concluding that because the concepts are simple, a custom implementation is safe. Audited libraries earn trust through years of scrutiny finding exactly these subtle bugs, not through the concepts being complex.

items.prompt: A team writes their own "constant-time" comparison function without testing it against timing analysis. What's the risk, specifically?
choices: None — writing it themselves guarantees they understand it correctly

It might not actually be constant-time in practice (compiler optimizations, early returns in helper functions, etc. can reintroduce timing variance) — a subtle implementation bug can silently defeat the exact protection it was meant to provide
Custom comparison functions are always faster than library ones
This risk only applies to hash functions, not comparison functions
items.explanation: "Constant-time" is a property that's easy to intend and surprisingly hard to guarantee in practice — the risk isn't that the concept is misunderstood, it's that a well-intentioned implementation can still leak timing information through paths the author didn't anticipate.

items.prompt: In L3's real code, `register()` calls `scryptSync(password, salt, 64)` while the rainbow-table demo's `unsaltedHash()` calls `createHash('sha256')`. Which one is the deliberately slow, tunable choice appropriate for password storage?
choices: createHash('sha256') — it's the newer API
scryptSync — it's a key-derivation function designed to be slow and resource-intensive, unlike sha256 which is a fast general-purpose hash never intended for password storage
Both are equally appropriate
Neither — both should be replaced with encryption
items.explanation: scrypt is purpose-built as a key-derivation function: deliberately slow and tunable. sha256 is a fast general-purpose hash, useful for things like data integrity checks, but the wrong tool for password storage precisely because of its speed.
items.reference:
scryptSync(password, salt, 64) — slow, tunable
createHash('sha256') — fast, wrong choice for passwords
items.learnMore:
Reading real crypto code for intent, not just syntax

The function name signals the design intent — knowing which primitive is which is what makes a code review catch a bad choice.

Use caseReal call
Password hashingscryptSync(password, salt, keylen)Slow, tunable, salted by convention
Integrity checks, non-secret datacreateHash('sha256')Fast, no built-in salting concept

Common mistake

Seeing `crypto` module usage and assuming it's automatically "secure enough" without checking which specific function was called — `createHash('sha256')` and `scryptSync` solve different problems.

items.prompt: In L3's code, `verifyLogin` re-derives `attemptHash` using `scryptSync(password, storedSalt, 64)` — the *stored* salt, not a new random one. Why must it reuse the stored salt rather than generating a fresh one for the login attempt?
choices: It doesn't matter which salt is used, as long as scrypt is used

Because the original hash was derived from the *original* salt — verification only works if the exact same salt is used to re-derive the hash, or even the correct password would produce a completely different (non-matching) result
Because generating a new salt is computationally expensive
Because scrypt requires the salt to be reused across all users
items.explanation: Hashing is deterministic only for a fixed input — password and salt together. Using a different salt at login than at registration would make even the correct password fail to reproduce the stored hash.

items.prompt: Implement a toy (non-cryptographic, for illustrating the mechanism only) `saltedHash(password, salt)` and use it to show the salting effect: it should combine `password` and `salt` into a single string and return a simple numeric hash. Two different salts applied to the SAME password must produce different results, and two different passwords with the SAME salt must also (in general) produce different results.

tests.description: same password, different salts, produces different hashes
same password AND same salt reproduces the identical hash (verification must be deterministic)
different passwords, same salt, produce different hashes

items.explanation: This is a toy hash (real systems use scrypt/bcrypt/Argon2, per L3), but it demonstrates the real property salting depends on: the function must be deterministic (same input always reproduces the same output, so login verification works) while still being sensitive enough to input changes that a different salt or password produces a different result — exactly the property that defeats precomputed lookup tables in the real rainbow-table demonstration in L3.
items.reference:
Required: deterministic — same input always → same output
Required: sensitive — changing password OR salt → different output
items.learnMore:
What a salted hash function actually has to guarantee

Real algorithms differ (scrypt vs. a toy running-sum), but the required properties don't.

PropertyWhat breaks without it
YesLogin verification would randomly failDeterministic
YesAll shared-password users get the same hashInput-sensitive (to salt and password)

Common mistake

Believing the specific mixing formula (sum, XOR, multiply) is what provides security. In toy exercises it's arbitrary — in production, the formula matters enormously (see L3's fast-vs-slow-hash distinction), but the two properties tested here (determinism, sensitivity) are what any correct implementation must have regardless.

items.prompt: Implement a different toy (non-cryptographic) `mixHash(salt, password)` — note the argument order is flipped from the first version: prepend `salt` before `password` and return a numeric hash using a running XOR-and-multiply mix (e.g. `hash = (hash * 33) ^ charCode` per character, seeded at 0). Same required properties: deterministic for identical input, sensitive to a change in either password or salt.

tests.description: same password, different salts, produces different hashes
same salt AND same password reproduces the identical hash (verification must be deterministic)
different passwords, same salt, produce different hashes

items.explanation: A different mixing formula (XOR-and-multiply instead of a running sum) still has to satisfy the same two properties as the first variant: determinism, so the exact same salt+password always verifies correctly, and sensitivity, so any change to either input changes the output. The specific arithmetic is interchangeable — real systems don't use hand-rolled mixes like this at all, per L3's warning against rolling a custom scheme — but the property being tested is the same one that makes salting work.
